scenarios.title: FORMAT EXAMPLE — replace with an original situation
scenarios.objective: Locate an outlet and approaching pressure before planning a retrieval.
scenarios.briefing: You are in Navy’s defensive zone, where Navy defends the nearby net. YOU are approaching a loose puck near the side boards. F2 is a possible outlet toward the middle; D1 is approaching from up ice. No player has recovered the puck yet.
cues: The puck is loose beside the wall.
F2 is away from the wall.
D1 approaches from the up-ice side.

sources.title: 7 Principles for Coaches: Vision & Scanning
sources.section: Key Information to Identify; Reading Pressure / Corner Situations
sources.use: Supports checking teammates and pressure; answers are original scene analysis.

scenarios.limits: Static original practice illustration; movement and outcomes are not simulated. A frozen picture cannot measure an actual shoulder check or the arrival order. Position references are examples, not graded target zones.

questions.prompt: What is true about possession at this freeze?
questions.explanation: The puck is drawn away from every blade and has no owner.

questions.prompt: Which two things would help YOU plan the pickup?

options.text: Only the loose puck, without checking the players

questions.explanation: An outlet and the approaching pressure inform the next action; neither guarantees a successful pickup.

options.text: Approach and control the loose puck
Check whether the outlet is still available

questions.explanation: This is a simple discussion routine. Real scanning may repeat throughout the approach.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to an approach point on the middle side of the wall-side puck.
questions.explanation: The example is 1.70 m from the puck and closer to rink middle than the puck. Recheck F2 and D1 before the touch; the marker does not prove where YOU look or whether possession is gained.

questions.prompt: Before planning a pass after the pickup, which relationship should YOU account for in this view?

options.text: D1 and F2 are both up ice from the loose puck
D1 is on the net side of the loose puck, opposite F2 along the rink

questions.explanation: Both the opponent D1 and teammate F2 are up ice from the loose puck. That puts pressure and the possible outlet in the area YOU need to read before recovery. It does not show who reaches the puck first or establish that a pass to F2 is clear.

questions.prompt: What would you want to see again just before touching this puck?
questions.explanation: Name a change in D1 or F2 that could alter the plan. Saying where you would look is more useful than simply saying “scan.”
